flashcards.q: Why is 'ECS vs Fargate' a category error?
flashcards.a: ECS/EKS are orchestrators (where/how containers are scheduled); EC2/Fargate are compute engines (what they run on). They're orthogonal axes — you can pair either orchestrator with either compute option, giving 4 real combinations, not 2.

flashcards.q: What's the EKS control-plane fee, and how does it compare to ECS?
flashcards.a: EKS: flat $0.10/hour (~$73/month) per cluster regardless of workload size. ECS: no control-plane fee at all. The fee can be a 400%+ tax on a tiny single-service cluster but shrinks to under 5% of spend at real fleet scale.

flashcards.q: Roughly what price premium does Fargate carry over equivalent EC2 capacity, and what is it buying?
flashcards.a: Commonly quoted in the 40-60% range above equivalent EC2 compute. It buys zero node management — no patching, capacity planning, or autoscaler tuning — a good trade for bursty/unpredictable workloads, a bad default for large steady-state fleets.

flashcards.q: What's the honest default recommendation for a new AWS-only team with no hard Kubernetes requirement?
flashcards.a: ECS + Fargate — simplest operational model, zero control-plane fee. Graduate to EKS only for a real, named requirement (multi-cloud, a specific k8s-only tool/operator, deliberate hiring/ecosystem bet), not by default.

flashcards.q: How does IAM authentication differ between an ECS task and an EKS pod?
flashcards.a: ECS: a task role is a normal IAM role directly assumed by the task, no federation layer. EKS: a ServiceAccount has no IAM identity by default — needs IRSA (OIDC federation) or EKS Pod Identity to get any AWS permissions at all.

flashcards.q: A pod on EKS can't reach S3 despite the referenced IAM role having correct permissions. First thing to check?
flashcards.a: Whether the ServiceAccount-to-IAM-role association (IRSA annotation or Pod Identity association) actually exists and is correctly configured, and whether the pod spec references that specific ServiceAccount — a correct policy is irrelevant if the federation link is missing.

flashcards.q: Can a DaemonSet run on an EKS Fargate profile? Why or why not, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: No — Fargate gives each pod isolated compute with no shared-node concept for a DaemonSet's one-per-node pattern to attach to. Sidecar containers are the standard replacement for logging/monitoring coverage on Fargate-profile pods.

flashcards.q: Why don't EKS worker nodes need imagePullSecrets to pull from ECR (same-account, same-region)?
flashcards.a: Authentication happens automatically via the node's own IAM role (or the Fargate task's execution role) — the node's AWS identity itself authenticates the pull, unlike a third-party registry which needs an explicit imagePullSecrets-referenced Secret.

flashcards.q: What happens to ECR images if no lifecycle policy is set?
flashcards.a: ECR retains every pushed image indefinitely by default — a slow, easy-to-miss storage cost leak. A lifecycle policy (e.g. keep last N tagged images, expire untagged after N days) is the standard fix.

flashcards.q: What does ECR pull-through cache solve, and what changes for pods using it?
flashcards.a: Lets ECR transparently proxy and cache images from upstream registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, Quay, Chainguard) so pulls hit ECR in-region instead of the public upstream, fixing rate-limit-driven ImagePullBackOff. Image references must change to the ECR-proxied path, not a transparent zero-touch change.

flashcards.q: When does the EKS control-plane fee actually become a trap, contrary to intuition?
flashcards.a: When a team runs many small EKS clusters instead of consolidating — the fixed ~$73/month fee multiplies across each small cluster, even though the aggregate workload might be large enough that a single larger cluster's fee would be negligible.

flashcards.q: What are the two ECR image scanning modes, and how do they differ?
flashcards.a: Basic scanning: Clair-based CVE detection at push time only. Enhanced scanning: integrates with Amazon Inspector for continuous rescanning as new CVEs are published against already-pushed images, not just at push time.

flashcards.q: Why can an EKS cluster fail to schedule pods on 'insufficient IP addresses' even with free CPU/memory on nodes?
flashcards.a: The default VPC CNI assigns each pod a real routable VPC IP, so pod density is bounded by ENI secondary-IP capacity and free subnet address space, independent of compute. Fix with larger subnets, prefix delegation (/28 prefixes instead of individual IPs), or an overlay-mode CNI.

flashcards.q: What's the core mechanical difference between Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter for EKS node provisioning?
flashcards.a: Cluster Autoscaler only scales pre-defined ASG node groups' size. Karpenter provisions nodes directly without ASGs, picking best-fit instance type/AZ per pending pod's actual resource requests at scheduling time, and actively consolidates underutilized nodes — faster scale-up, better bin-packing, bounded by NodePool/EC2NodeClass constraints.
